title: Analysis and Reproducibility
description: Interpret statistical evidence and make research auditable.

questions.prompt: A p-value is the probability of:
options: Data at least this extreme under a specified null model
questions.explanation: It is conditional on the null model and assumptions, not the probability the hypothesis is true.

questions.prompt: A p-value below .05 means the null hypothesis has only a 5% chance of being true.
questions.explanation: That reverses conditional probability; p-values do not directly give posterior hypothesis probabilities.

questions.prompt: Which improve reproducibility?
questions.explanation: Code, decision records, and computational details help others inspect and reproduce analyses.

questions.prompt: A confidence interval communicates estimate precision under a statistical procedure.
questions.explanation: Interpretation depends on assumptions; it is not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in this interval.

questions.prompt: A type I error is:
options: Failing to reject a false null
questions.explanation: It is a false positive relative to the specified null and decision rule.

questions.prompt: A nonsignificant result proves two conditions are exactly equivalent.
questions.explanation: Failure to reject a difference does not establish equivalence; that requires margins and an appropriate design.

questions.prompt: Which can inflate false-positive risk?
options: Repeated significance checks with opportunistic stopping
questions.explanation: Unaccounted multiplicity and selective choices increase false-positive risk; preregistration discloses plans.

questions.prompt: Effect size describes the magnitude of an observed difference or association.
questions.explanation: Magnitude complements uncertainty and practical context; scale matters.

questions.prompt: A power analysis can help researchers:
questions.explanation: Power analysis informs sample size and detectable effects but depends on assumptions and design.

questions.prompt: A larger sample can improve precision but cannot repair a systematically biased measure.
questions.explanation: More observations reduce random error, not systematic bias.

questions.prompt: Which support a transparent report?
questions.explanation: Complete reporting helps readers evaluate analytic flexibility and selective disclosure.

questions.prompt: Data-cleaning decisions should be documented because they can affect results.
questions.explanation: Handling outliers, missingness, and coding can change estimates and should be traceable.

questions.prompt: A type II error is:
options: Failing to detect an effect that exists
questions.explanation: It is a false negative under a defined alternative and design.

questions.prompt: Statistical significance alone establishes that a finding is replicable.
questions.explanation: Replication depends on effect stability, design, measurement, and context.

questions.prompt: Which help manage missing data responsibly?
options: Replace every missing value with zero
questions.explanation: Missingness patterns and assumptions matter; simplistic replacement can distort estimates.

questions.prompt: Preregistration prevents all analytic flexibility.
questions.explanation: Researchers may need justified changes; transparent documentation distinguishes deviations from plans.

questions.prompt: An outlier is:
options: An observation unusually distant from others
A value that must be removed
questions.explanation: Outliers need investigation; they may be valid cases, errors, or influential observations.

questions.prompt: Which promote computational reproducibility?
questions.explanation: Versioning, data documentation, and controlled randomness make computations easier to recreate.

questions.prompt: Open data should be shared even when it contains identifiable sensitive information.
questions.explanation: Privacy, consent, and legal duties can limit sharing; de-identification or controlled access may be appropriate.

questions.prompt: A statistically clear result can still be too uncertain or small to guide a practical decision.
questions.explanation: Decision relevance depends on magnitude, uncertainty, costs, and context.
